provenance.note: Cardiovascular Semiology 4 (Angina Pectoris).pdf (Pr. Anh Tuan Dinh Xuan, Cardiovascular Semiology, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Angina: transient ischaemia, no infarction.
Stable: plaque over 70 percent, exertional, relieved by rest, ST depression.
Unstable: clot on plaque, pain at rest, emergency.
Prinzmetal: spasm, at rest or night, ST elevation.
Elderly: epigastric pain after meals; women: burning.
Prinzmetal test: ergonovine or acetylcholine.
Treatment: sublingual nitroglycerin, nitrates, aspirin, beta blockers, CCBs.

deeper.title: Why unstable angina is treated like a heart attack in progress
deeper.html:
In unstable angina, a clot has formed on the plaque. The same clot that narrows the artery at rest can grow and block it completely at any moment, turning ischaemia into infarction. That is why the lecture calls it an emergency, even though no muscle has yet died.

Source: the lecture's unstable angina slides.

provenance.note: Cardiovascular Semiology 5 (Arrhythmia).pdf (Pr. Anh Tuan Dinh Xuan, Cardiovascular Semiology, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: AFib: commonest significant arrhythmia; about 59 million in 2019.
Conduction: SA node, atria, AV node, His, Purkinje.
P atrial, QRS ventricular (0.08 to 0.12 s), T repolarisation.
AFib ECG: no P waves, irregularly irregular.
Flutter: 250 to 350/min, sawtooth F waves, often regular.
AFib clots in the left atrial appendage; stroke risk five-fold.
AFib causes: hypertension, CAD, mitral disease, heart failure.

deeper.title: Why an irregularly irregular pulse matters
deeper.html:
A pulse with no pattern at all is the bedside sign of atrial fibrillation, which may otherwise be silent. Because AFib multiplies stroke risk, feeling for irregularity in every patient's pulse is one of the cheapest stroke-prevention tools in medicine.

Source: the lecture's AFib symptoms and stroke slides.

provenance.note: Cardiovascular Semiology 1 (Introduction).pdf (Pr. Anh Tuan Dinh Xuan, Cardiovascular Semiology, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Rest 3 to 5 min before vital signs; bare arm; not the mastectomy side.
Vertical sternal scar = prior open-heart surgery.
Pectus deformity + hypermobility: think Marfan.
Xanthelasma: hypercholesterolaemia.
Roth spots, Osler nodes (painful), Janeway (painless), splinters: endocarditis.
Cyanosis at Hb 10 needs about 70 percent saturation.
JVP: right IJV, 15 to 45 degrees, positive over 4 cm above sternal angle.
JVD reflects right heart and CVP, not dehydration.

deeper.title: Why cyanosis can hide in anaemia
deeper.html:
Cyanosis appears when enough haemoglobin is deoxygenated in absolute terms. With little haemoglobin, even very low saturation leaves too little deoxygenated haemoglobin to turn skin blue. So an anaemic patient can be dangerously hypoxic without cyanosis, and if cyanosis does appear, the situation is critical.

Source: the lecture's cyanosis slide.

provenance.note: Cardiovascular Semiology 2 (Left Heart Failure).pdf (Pr. Anh Tuan Dinh Xuan, Cardiovascular Semiology, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Systolic HF: can't pump, thin chambers, EF 40 percent or less.
Diastolic HF: can't fill, thick stiff chambers, EF normal.
SV = EDV minus ESV; CO = HR x SV, about 5 L/min.
Normal EF 64 to 70 percent.
Frank-Starling: more preload, bigger stroke volume.
RAAS causes fluid retention.
Diastolic causes: hypertension, aortic stenosis, HCM, restrictive CM.
LHF gives pulmonary oedema: orthopnoea, PND, crackles, frothy sputum.

deeper.title: Why heart failure patients sleep on several pillows
deeper.html:
Lying flat returns more blood from the legs to the chest, which a failing left ventricle cannot handle, so pressure rises in the pulmonary veins and fluid floods the lungs. Sitting up lets gravity pool blood in the legs, easing the congestion. That is orthopnoea, and asking how many pillows a patient needs is a quick measure of its severity.

Source: the lecture's pulmonary oedema slides.

provenance.note: Cardiovascular Semiology 6 (Revision).pdf (Pr. Anh Tuan Dinh Xuan, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the revision slides. This lecture reviews heart failure and angina, covered in full on their own pages, and adds haemodynamics, coronary flow, endothelial dysfunction and the global burden of cardiovascular disease. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Q = ΔP / R.
Left coronary flow mainly in diastole.
NO relaxes vessels; endothelial dysfunction leads to atherothrombosis.
CVD: leading cause of death, about 17.7 million/year.
High-income countries: cancer kills twice as many as CVD.
Over 70 percent of CVD from modifiable risk factors.

deeper.title: Why a fast heart rate can starve the heart
deeper.html:
The left coronary artery fills mostly in diastole. As heart rate rises, diastole shortens much more than systole, so the heart gets less time to feed itself just when it works hardest. That is one reason tachycardia can trigger angina in someone with narrowed coronaries.

Source: the lecture's coronary flow slide, with standard physiology.

provenance.note: Cardiovascular Semiology 3 (Right Heart Failure).pdf (Pr. Anh Tuan Dinh Xuan, Cardiovascular Semiology, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: RHF most often caused by LHF.
ASD and VSD: left-to-right shunt overloads the right heart.
Cor pulmonale: lung disease, hypoxic vasoconstriction, pulmonary hypertension.
Chronic hypoxia causes polycythaemia.
RHF signs: JVD, hepatosplenomegaly, ascites, dependent oedema.
Oedema: ankles standing, sacrum lying.
Pitting grades 1 to 4: 2, 3 to 4, 5 to 6, 8 mm.
Liver congestion can progress to cardiac cirrhosis.

deeper.title: Why a bedbound patient's oedema is in the back, not the ankles
deeper.html:
Oedema follows gravity to the lowest point. Standing, that is the ankles and legs; lying in bed, it is the sacrum and lower back. Examining only the ankles of a bedbound patient can miss significant fluid overload.

Source: the lecture's pitting oedema slide.

provenance.note: adrenal semiology 2026.pdf, converted from the PowerPoint (Endocrinology semiology, Pr. Ioana Hristov, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Partial page. Most slides in this 28 MB PowerPoint are images, so only the readable text is covered: Cushing's syndrome, its ACTH-based classification, and adrenal and catecholamine imaging. A PDF export of the slides would let this page be completed. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Cushing's syndrome: cortisol excess of any cause; Cushing's disease: pituitary.
Truncal obesity, moon face, purple striae, limb atrophy.
Hypertension, diabetes, osteoporosis, thrombosis, depression.
High ACTH: pituitary or ectopic; low ACTH: adrenal.
MIBG: catecholamine-secreting tissue.

deeper.title: Why low ACTH points to the adrenal
deeper.html:
Cortisol normally switches ACTH off by feedback. If an adrenal tumour makes cortisol on its own, ACTH is suppressed. If ACTH is high despite high cortisol, something is driving the adrenals: a pituitary or ectopic source.

Source: the lecture's cortisol excess algorithm, with standard physiology.

provenance.note: DIABETES SEMIOLOGY 2026.pdf, converted from the PowerPoint (Endocrinology semiology, Pr. Ioana Hristov, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. On the 10 November midterm: only the symptoms that reveal diabetes. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Diabetes: chronic hyperglycaemia from lack of insulin secretion and/or action.
Found by chance, from hyperglycaemia symptoms, or at a complication.
Polyuria from osmotic diuresis; polydipsia from the polyuria; weight loss from lipolysis.
Classic syndrome: polyuria, polydipsia, polyphagia, weight loss.
Glycosuria appears above 1.8 g/L.
Criteria: fasting ≥ 1.26 g/L twice; OGTT 2 h ≥ 2 g/L; HbA1c ≥ 6.5%; random ≥ 2 g/L with symptoms.
Type 1: young, thin, acute, ketosis, autoimmune.
Type 2: over 40, family history, overweight, progressive, found late or at a complication.
Type 2 is 85 to 90% of diabetes.

deeper.title: Why thirst follows the urine, not the other way round
deeper.html:
Above about 1.8 g/L the kidney can no longer reabsorb all the filtered glucose. The glucose left in the tubule holds water with it (osmotic diuresis), so large volumes of urine are passed. The water loss then triggers thirst. In primary polydipsia the order is reversed: drinking comes first and the urine follows.

Source: the lecture's history and examination slides, with standard renal physiology.

provenance.note: PITUITARY FINAL SEMIOLOGY 2026.pdf, converted from the PowerPoint (Endocrinology semiology, Pr. Ioana Hristov, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. On the 10 November midterm: acromegaly, prolactinoma and pituitary mass effect only. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Pituitary disease: hypersecretion of an axis, insufficiency, mass effect.
Prolactin excess: galactorrhoea and amenorrhoea in women; low libido first in men.
Prolactin: PEG precipitation for macroprolactin, then pituitary MRI.
Metoclopramide and other dopamine antagonists raise prolactin.
Acromegaly: frontal bossing, prognathism, macroglossia, big hands and feet, oily sweaty skin.
Acromegaly: carpal tunnel in up to half; sleep apnoea, colonic polyps, LVH, diabetes.
Acromegaly is confirmed by high IGF-1 and no GH suppression on a 75 g OGTT.
Chiasm compression: bitemporal loss, superior fields first.
Cavernous sinus: III, IV, VI palsy, so diplopia and ptosis.
Apoplexy: sudden headache, visual loss, ophthalmoplegia; emergency.

deeper.title: Why chiasm compression is bitemporal
deeper.html:
At the chiasm, the fibres from each nasal half-retina cross to the other side. The nasal retina sees the temporal visual field, so pressing on those crossing fibres takes out both temporal fields. A tumour pushing up from below meets the lower fibres first, which carry the upper fields: that is why the loss starts in the superior quadrants.

Source: the lecture's mass-effect slides, with standard neuroanatomy.

provenance.note: thyroid semiology 2026.pdf, converted from the PowerPoint (Endocrinology semiology, Pr. Ioana Hristov, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Normal thyroid not visible; bruit = hyperthyroid high flow.
Hyper: TSH low; hypo: TSH high.
Graves': commonest, TRAb, thyrotoxicosis + goitre + exophthalmos.
Toxic adenoma: hot nodule, no eye signs.
Jod-Basedow: hyperthyroidism after iodine.
Hypo labs: macrocytic anaemia, hyponatraemia, high cholesterol.
Iodine deficiency: endemic goitre.
Goitre over 18 cm³ (F) or 20 cm³ (M).
FNAC for U3 to U5 nodules.

deeper.title: Why TSH moves opposite to thyroid hormone
deeper.html:
TSH is controlled by negative feedback: when thyroid hormone is high, the pituitary shuts TSH off; when it is low, TSH rises to push the gland harder. So in primary thyroid disease TSH moves the opposite way and is the most sensitive single test. Only in pituitary (central) disease do both fall together.

Source: the lecture's thyroid function slides, with standard physiology.

provenance.note: GI BLEEDING SEMIO 26.27 CANVAS.pdf (Digestive semiology, Prof. O. Bahlaoui, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: GI bleeding is a vital emergency: assess severity first.
Haematemesis: lesion above the angle of Treitz.
Melaena: digested blood, usually upper GI, appears 6-8 h after onset.
Haematochezia: usually lower GI, or massive upper bleed.
Normal Hb does not exclude recent bleeding.
Two large-bore IV lines, group and cross-match, fluids, transfusion, oxygen.
Upper endoscopy first line; finds the source in > 90%.
Colonoscopy is the key test for lower bleeding.
Upper causes: ulcer, varices, Mallory-Weiss, gastritis, cancer, NSAIDs.
Lower causes: haemorrhoids, fissure, cancer, polyps, diverticula, angiodysplasia, IBD, Meckel's.
Endoscopic haemostasis: injection, coagulation, clips, band ligation.

deeper.title: Why haemoglobin can be normal in a major bleed
deeper.html:
Blood is lost whole: red cells and plasma leave together, so the concentration of haemoglobin is unchanged at first. It only falls hours later, when fluid from the tissues and infusions dilute the remaining blood. Pulse, blood pressure and perfusion therefore judge the severity of an acute bleed better than the first haemoglobin.

Source: the lecture's biological evaluation slide.

deeper.title: Why melaena is black
deeper.html:
Blood that passes slowly through the stomach and small bowel is exposed to acid and bacteria, which turn haemoglobin into black haematin. That takes hours, which is why melaena appears 6 to 8 hours after an upper bleed. Blood from the lower colon has no time to change and stays red.

Source: the lecture's melaena slide.

provenance.note: constipation.pdf (Digestive semiology, Pr. Wafaa Khannoussi and Dr Afafe Taiymi)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Constipation: under 3 stools/week, under 100 g/day, hard stools.
Primary: slow transit or outlet dysfunction.
Outlet: pelvic floor fails to relax (anismus).
Absent bowel sounds: ileus; hyperactive: obstruction.
Red flags: bleeding, weight loss, anaemia, family history.
Causes: hypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, opioids, iron.
Anorectal manometry: dyssynergic defecation.

deeper.title: Why new constipation in an older adult is taken seriously
deeper.html:
A change in bowel habit late in life may be the first sign of colorectal cancer narrowing the colon. That is why new-onset constipation, especially with bleeding, weight loss or anaemia, prompts colonoscopy rather than just laxatives.

Source: the lecture's red flags and work-up slides.

provenance.note: DIARRHEA SEMIO 26.27 CANVAS.pdf (Digestive semiology, Prof. O. Bahlaoui, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Diarrhoea: > 300 g/day, > 3 stools/day, > 90% water.
Acute < 2 weeks; prolonged 2-4 weeks; chronic > 4 weeks.
Choleriform: toxin, watery, persists fasting. Dysenteric: invasive, blood, fever, tenesmus.
Dangerous in infants, elderly, immunocompromised.
Antibiotics → think C. difficile.
Tests in acute diarrhoea only if severe, bloody, febrile, > 3 days, epidemic or immunosuppressed.
Digital rectal examination is mandatory in chronic diarrhoea.
Anti-transglutaminase antibodies and duodenal biopsies for coeliac disease.
Osmotic and motor stop/improve with fasting; secretory persists.
Malabsorption: greasy, pale, foul stools.
Exudative diarrhoea: alpha-1 antitrypsin clearance.

deeper.title: Why the fasting test separates osmotic from secretory diarrhoea
deeper.html:
Osmotic diarrhoea is caused by something the patient eats that stays in the lumen and holds water; stop eating and the water stops. Secretory diarrhoea comes from the gut wall actively pumping out salt and water, driven by a toxin, hormone or inflammation, which continues regardless of food. That simple observation narrows the list of causes dramatically.

Source: the lecture's synthetic comparison table.

deeper.title: Why dysenteric stools contain blood
deeper.html:
Invasive bacteria penetrate and destroy the colonic mucosa, producing ulcers that bleed and inflammatory exudate rich in mucus and pus. Inflammation of the rectum also causes tenesmus, the painful urge to pass stool with little output. Toxin-mediated diarrhoea leaves the mucosa intact, which is why it is watery rather than bloody.

Source: the lecture's pathophysiological types slide.

figure.caption: Duration, then mechanism. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: Dysentery.pdf (Digestive semiology, Pr. Wafaa Khannoussi and Dr Afafe Taiymi)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Dysentery: pain, frequent mucus-blood-pus stools, false urges.
Reflects rectal inflammation, infection or neoplasia.
Tenesmus: painful urge, empty rectum.
Pain often in the left iliac fossa.
C. difficile toxin after antibiotics.
Stool culture: Shigella, Salmonella, Campylobacter, E. coli.
Sigmoidoscopy confirms and allows biopsy.
Causes: cancer, IBD, infection, radiation, ischaemia.

deeper.title: Why dysentery is not the same as diarrhoea
deeper.html:
Watery diarrhoea usually comes from the small bowel losing fluid. Dysentery comes from an inflamed rectum and colon, so stools are small, frequent and made of mucus, pus and blood, with tenesmus. That distinction points you to the colon and to endoscopy.

Source: the lecture's definition and symptoms slides.

provenance.note: DYSPHAGIA SEMIO 26.27 CANVAS.pdf (Digestive semiology, Prof. O. Bahlaoui, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Dysphagia = difficulty swallowing; odynophagia = pain; aphagia = inability; globus = lump sensation.
Progressive dysphagia in an adult = oesophageal cancer until proven otherwise.
Upper GI endoscopy is first line.
Oropharyngeal: cough, nasal regurgitation. Oesophageal: food stuck behind the sternum.
Solids then liquids → organic; liquids ≥ solids (paradoxical) → motor.
Achalasia: absent peristalsis + non-relaxing LES on manometry.
Examine cranial nerves IX to XII.
Red flags: > 50 years, rapid progression, weight loss > 5 kg, iron-deficiency anaemia.
Complications: aspiration pneumonia, malnutrition, aphagia, perforation.

deeper.title: Why cancer makes solids stick first
deeper.html:
A growing tumour narrows the lumen gradually. At first only a solid bolus is too large to pass; liquids still flow around it. As the stricture tightens, even liquids stop, and the patient ends up unable to swallow saliva. That steady, progressive pattern is the signature of mechanical obstruction.

Source: the lecture's history-taking and cancer slides.

deeper.title: Why achalasia makes liquids stick as much as solids
deeper.html:
In achalasia the problem is not a narrow lumen but a sphincter that will not open and an oesophagus that no longer pushes. Everything, liquid or solid, depends on gravity and pressure building up above the closed sphincter. That is why liquids can be as difficult as solids from the start, and why symptoms come and go.

Source: the lecture's achalasia slide.

figure.caption: Level first, then mechanism. Schematic drawn for this site.

provenance.note: digestive physical examination.pdf (Digestive semiology, Pr. Wafaa Khannoussi)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Doctor stands on the patient's right.
Glossitis: B12; angular cheilitis: iron.
Left supraclavicular node: digestive cancer.
Collateral veins: portal hypertension.
Eventration: hernia on a scar.
Deep breath lowers the liver.
Dull over the liver; rest tympanic.
Rectal exam: knee-chest or Sims.

deeper.title: Why the left supraclavicular node matters
deeper.html:
Lymph from the abdomen drains via the thoracic duct, which empties near the left supraclavicular region. A hard node there can be the first sign of a stomach or other digestive cancer that has spread, so it is always felt during a digestive exam.

Source: the lecture's cervical examination slide, with standard anatomy.

provenance.note: GERD semiology 26.27 CANVAS.pdf (Digestive semiology, Prof. O. Bahlaoui, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. Slides that only show pictures are covered in outline. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: GERD: reflux causing symptoms and/or complications.
Barrier: LES + diaphragmatic crura.
Hiatal hernia is the commonest anatomical cause.
Typical symptoms: pyrosis and regurgitation.
Typical forms: diagnosis is clinical.
Extra-digestive: chronic cough, hoarseness, dental erosions, non-cardiac chest pain.
Alarm signs → endoscopy.
Normal endoscopy does not exclude GERD (NERD).
pH-metry: pH < 4 for > 5% of the time.
Complications: oesophagitis, bleeding, stricture, Barrett's.

deeper.title: Why reflux is worse lying down and at night
deeper.html:
Standing, gravity keeps gastric contents in the stomach and swallowed saliva washes the oesophagus. Lying down removes gravity, swallowing becomes rare during sleep, and acid stays in contact with the mucosa longer. That is why the lecture lists nocturnal symptoms, bending and lying down as classic triggers.

Source: the lecture's pyrosis slide.

deeper.title: Why GERD can cause a cough without heartburn
deeper.html:
Tiny amounts of refluxed acid can reach the larynx and be aspirated into the airways, and acid in the lower oesophagus can trigger a vagal cough reflex. Some patients therefore present with chronic cough, hoarseness or asthma-like symptoms and little heartburn, which is why the lecture insists on considering GERD in chronic cough or dysphonia.

Source: the lecture's extra-digestive manifestations slides.

figure.caption: Mechanism, symptoms, alarm signs and complications. Schematic drawn for this site.
labels: Risk factors: hiatal hernia, obesity, pregnancy, drugs

provenance.note: Hepatomegaly.pdf (Digestive semiology, Pr. Wafaa Khannoussi)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Hepatomegaly: diagnosis is clinical.
Normal liver span under 12 cm (midclavicular).
Ultrasound first-line.
Cirrhosis: hard, nodular, painless.
Cardiac: soft, smooth, painful, hepatojugular reflux.
Abscess: intensely painful.
Riedel lobe is a right-sided differential.
HMG + neuro signs: Wilson's.

deeper.title: Why the congested liver hurts but the cirrhotic one does not
deeper.html:
Pain comes from stretching of the liver capsule. Acute congestion in heart failure swells the liver quickly, stretching the capsule and causing pain. Cirrhosis develops slowly, with scarring and nodules, so the capsule is not suddenly stretched and the liver is usually painless.

Source: the lecture's clinical orientation table, with standard pathophysiology.

provenance.note: JAUNDICE.pdf (Digestive semiology, Pr. Wafaa Khannoussi)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Jaundice: bilirubin above about 35 µmol/L.
Bilirubin from haemoglobin breakdown.
Diagnosis is clinical.
Cholestasis: pruritus, dark urine, pale stools; GGT and ALP up.
Prolonged PT from vitamin K malabsorption.
Cholangitis: pain, fever, jaundice.
First step: cholestatic vs non-cholestatic.
Ultrasound: dilated ducts means extrahepatic obstruction.

deeper.title: Why urine darkens but stools pale
deeper.html:
In obstruction, conjugated bilirubin cannot reach the gut, so stools lose their colour. Being water-soluble, it spills into the blood and is filtered into urine, which darkens. Unconjugated bilirubin in haemolysis is bound to albumin and does not reach urine.

Source: the lecture's cholestasis slides, with standard physiology.

provenance.note: Nausea - Vomiting (Digestive semiology, Pr Afafe Taiymi, 2026-2027)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Vomiting: forceful, active expulsion of stomach contents; usually preceded by nausea.
Triggers: GI irritation, vestibular, cortical, CTZ (drugs, toxins).
During vomiting the LES relaxes and the diaphragm and abdominal muscles contract.
Morning: pregnancy, alcohol. Late postprandial: pyloric or duodenal obstruction. During meals: psychogenic.
Undigested food: gastroparesis or outlet obstruction. Feculent: bowel obstruction.
Hyperactive bowel sounds: obstruction; absent: ileus.
Headache + papilledema: raised intracranial pressure.
Alarm: haematemesis, bilious or feculent vomiting, weight loss, neurological signs, elderly, immunocompromised.
Labs: CBC, electrolytes, renal function, glucose (DKA), hCG, urine ketones.
Regurgitation and rumination: without nausea.
Gastroparesis: often diabetes.
Complications: hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia, metabolic alkalosis; Mallory-Weiss, Boerhaave; aspiration pneumonia.

deeper.title: Why vomiting causes metabolic alkalosis and hypokalaemia
deeper.html:
Gastric juice is rich in hydrochloric acid. Each vomit removes H+ and Cl-, so bicarbonate accumulates in the blood: metabolic alkalosis. Fluid loss activates aldosterone, which makes the kidney retain sodium and excrete potassium, and alkalosis shifts potassium into cells. Hence the lecture's triad of hypokalaemia, hyponatraemia and metabolic alkalosis, and the ECG to look for the rhythm effects of hypokalaemia.

Source: general physiology, linking the lecture's complications and ECG slides.

deeper.title: Mallory-Weiss versus Boerhaave
deeper.html:
Both follow forceful vomiting. In Mallory-Weiss the tear stays in the mucosa at the gastro-oesophageal junction: the patient vomits blood, usually after several non-bloody vomits, and the bleeding often stops on its own. In Boerhaave the oesophageal wall ruptures, contents leak into the mediastinum, and the patient becomes very ill with chest pain and shock: a surgical emergency.

Source: the lecture's mechanical complications slide; StatPearls on Mallory-Weiss syndrome.

provenance.note: Semiology 2 clinical examination 2025.pdf (Respiratory semiology, Prof. Nahid Zaghba, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Four steps: inspection, palpation, percussion, auscultation.
Normal adult RR 12 to 20.
Barrel chest: emphysema, asthma.
Clubbing: Lovibond 180 degrees or more; chronic hypoxaemia.
Horner: miosis, ptosis, anhidrosis.
Fremitus up in pneumonia; down in effusion, pneumothorax.
Dull: effusion, consolidation. Hyperresonant: pneumothorax, emphysema.
Fine crackles: fibrosis, oedema; coarse: infection.
Rub: foot in fresh snow; stridor: upper airway.
Consolidation: dull + bronchial breathing + increased resonance.

deeper.title: Why effusion and consolidation both sound dull but feel different
deeper.html:
Both fluid in the pleura and a solid, infected lung block the air that normally makes the chest resonant, so both are dull. But solid lung conducts voice vibrations well, so fremitus and vocal resonance rise, while fluid between lung and wall damps them. That single palpation step separates the two at the bedside.

Source: the lecture's palpation, percussion and summary table.

deeper.title: Why clubbing sends you looking for lung cancer
deeper.html:
Clubbing reflects chronic hypoxaemia or certain chronic diseases, and when it becomes painful with periostitis (Pierre Marie osteoarthropathy) it is often paraneoplastic. A smoker with new clubbing needs a chest X-ray.

Source: the lecture's clubbing and osteoarthropathy slides.

provenance.note: Semiology 1 Clinical symptoms 2025.pdf (Respiratory semiology, Prof. Nahid Zaghba, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Cough: acute under 3 weeks, chronic over 8.
Chronic bronchitis: 3 months a year for 2 years.
ACE inhibitors cause dry cough.
Bitonal cough: recurrent nerve.
Bronchorrhoea over 100 mL/day.
Vomica: clear = hydatid; chocolate = amoebic.
Hemoptysis: bright red frothy with cough; always an emergency.
High-abundance hemoptysis over 500 mL; 15 percent idiopathic.
Pericarditis relieved leaning forward; dissection radiates to the back.
Normal RR 16/min; expiratory dyspnoea = low obstruction.

deeper.title: Why ACE inhibitors cause a cough
deeper.html:
ACE also breaks down bradykinin. Blocking it lets bradykinin build up in the airways, where it sensitises the cough receptors, producing a persistent dry cough in a fair number of patients. Stopping the drug is the fix.

Source: the lecture's chronic dry cough causes, with standard pharmacology.

deeper.title: Why every hemoptysis is treated as an emergency
deeper.html:
The danger in hemoptysis is less blood loss than drowning: blood flooding the airways blocks gas exchange. A small bleed can herald a large one, and the cause may be cancer or tuberculosis, which is why the lecture insists the amount does not change the significance.

Source: the lecture's hemoptysis slides.

provenance.note: Semiology 3 Thoracic syndromes 2025.pdf (Respiratory semiology, Prof. Nahid Zaghba, 2025-2026)

body.build_note: Built from the lecture slides. If your professor says something different, trust your professor.
exam_points: Effusion: dull, fremitus down, meniscus opacity; large one pushes trachea away.
Thoracentesis above the lower rib.
Exudate albumin over 30 g/L; transudate under 30.
Pneumothorax: hyperresonant, visceral pleural line, lucency without markings.
Hydropneumothorax: opacity topped by lucency.
Consolidation: fremitus up, dull, air bronchogram.
Retracted opacity pulls structures toward it.
Pink puffer = panlobular; blue bloater = centrilobular.
Bronchiectasis: permanent dilatation, morning bronchorrhoea.
SVC syndrome: face and neck oedema; Pancoast-Tobias = Horner + apex tumour + bone lysis.

deeper.title: Why the trachea tells you effusion from collapse
deeper.html:
A large effusion adds volume to one side and pushes the mediastinum and trachea away. A retracted consolidation from a blocked bronchus removes volume and pulls them toward it. Both look white on the X-ray, so the position of the trachea is the quickest clue to which one you face.

Source: the lecture's effusion and retracted consolidation slides.

deeper.title: Why the needle goes above the rib
deeper.html:
The intercostal vein, artery and nerve run along the lower border of each rib. Inserting the needle just above the lower rib keeps it away from that bundle, avoiding bleeding and nerve injury during thoracentesis.

Source: the lecture's thoracentesis technique slide.
